Personnel Psychology, 76(1), 5-40. DOI 10.1111/peps.12514. PDF opened: https://www.Gwern.net/doc/sociology/technology/2022-ravid.pdf. Note: not Journal of Applied Psychology. date_and_recency: Received 10 Sept 2020, accepted 3 April 2022, published in Personnel Psychology vol 76 (2023). Literature window ends around 2020-2021; predates modern wellbeing-tracking and AI monitoring tools. Exact search cutoff not recorded here [uncertain].
key_claims: Across 94 independent samples, EPM presence shows no performance benefit and is associated with higher stress/strain. The stress link holds across monitoring purpose, invasiveness and synchronicity; no level of any moderator differed significantly. More invasive and less transparent monitoring gives more negative attitudes. Authors say EPM should be treated as a job demand and recommend monitoring narrowly, transparently and with monitoring-free recovery breaks. On the question asked: the paper does not test monitoring of wellbeing signals as such. It codes 'Admin/Safety' purpose (including health and safety and police body cameras) and finds stress still elevated there.
headline_figures: K = 94 samples, N = 23,461 (overall). Stress/strain, all EPM: K = 23, N = 5,022, corrected rho = .16, 95% CI [.13, .20]. Experimental studies: K = 19, rho = .18; non-experiment K = 4, rho = .16 (r .15). Physiological stress: K = 4, N = 859, rho = .23, CI [.06, .40]. By communicated purpose, stress/strain: Performance K = 9, N = 953, rho = .22 [.12, .32]; Admin/Safety K = 7, N = 1,425, rho = .16 [.07, .24] (without police body-worn cameras K = 6, rho = .16 [.06, .27]); Surveillance K = 6, N = 657, rho = .16 [.05, .28]; Development: zero studies. Higher invasiveness: rho = .20 [.10, .29]; breadth rho = .22 [.12, .31]; burnout subset rho = .18 [.06, .30]. Broad performance: K = 41, N = 5,804, rho = -.01, CI [-.05, .04]; task performance K = 28, rho = .00 [-.06, .06]. Privacy invasion K = 8, rho = .28. Effect sizes described as small to modest, similar to telework and high-performance work practices meta-analyses.
sample_unit_and_population: 94 independent samples, N = 23,461, mixed field and lab studies (Degree analysis K = 44: 25 field, 19 lab). Mostly monitoring experiments for stress (19 of 23). Workers of many kinds, including call centres, office workers, police and student or lab participants. Not software-engineer specific [uncertain on exact occupational mix, not tabulated in the text read].
observed_vs_stated: Mixed. Stress outcomes include self-reported anxiety, perceived stress, fatigue and performance pressure plus 4 studies with physiological indicators (e.g. heart rate). Performance outcomes are largely observed behaviour from lab experiments. Many studies used single-method measurement.
what_it_measures_or_defines: Stress/strain as a synthetic construct: broad stress/strain, anxiety, perceived stress, physiological indicators, burnout as a subset. EPM defined as 'the use of technological means to observe, record, and analyze information that directly or indirectly relates to employee job performance'.
mechanism_or_cause: Authors invoke Zajonc's mere-presence arousal and the job-demands framework: monitoring is an added demand with physiological and psychological costs. Invasiveness removes control and autonomy (Karasek). Uncertainty about data use and purpose adds role-related stress.
interventions_and_effects: No intervention tested; the paper compares monitoring characteristics. Recommendations, not tested effects: monitor narrowly; be transparent about what is collected and who sees it; give workers control (e.g. turn monitoring off at breaks); provide monitoring-free recovery periods. Transparency and constraints/control improved attitudes (broad attitudes with constraints/target control rho = .17 in the table read) but too few studies (K = 2) tested transparency on stress. Development or coaching-purpose monitoring is untested for stress.
transfer_to_software_teams: General workforce evidence, not software-specific. Plausible transfer to knowledge workers monitored by dashboards or activity trackers but most studies are older and lab-based. Does not cover self-report wellbeing surveys or pulse checks.
limitations_stated: "Several aspects of the EPM typology could not be tested due to absence of primary studies (K < 3) and caution should be exercised when interpreting results that are based on a relatively small number of primary studies (e.g., K < 5)." Synthetic constructs add between-study variance; EPM characteristics covary and power was limited to separate them; purpose coded from the stated purpose, not worker perception; single-method measurement and file-drawer risk.
counter_evidence: Development-purpose monitoring has no stress data, so the paper cannot say supportive monitoring is stressful. Admin/Safety stress effect (rho .16) is similar to other purposes, which is the closest proxy for 'wellbeing monitoring', but only 7 studies, one block being police body cameras. Authors note that Admin/Safety attitudes were neutral (rho about .01) and performance unaffected. Effects are small to modest, correlational at the study-aggregate level, and heavily lab-based. Wellbeing-signal monitoring by employers (wearables, sentiment tools) is barely studied: authors found only two health-and-safety studies.
verification_status: All figures and quotes above checked against the opened full-text PDF (Personnel Psychology version): verified. The claim that the paper tests wellbeing-signal monitoring is explicitly NOT supported: [uncertain]/not tested. Funding statement not located [uncertain].
usable_claim: A 2022 meta-analysis of 94 samples (23,461 people) found that being electronically monitored was associated with higher stress (corrected correlation .16) and no performance gain, and the stress link held whatever the stated purpose, including health and safety. It did not test monitoring of wellbeing signals directly, and the authors say research on health-and-safety and development-oriented monitoring is thin. So it is reasonable to say monitoring is no automatic stress relief, not that wellbeing monitoring backfires.
do_not_use: Do not claim the paper shows wellbeing or burnout monitoring backfires. Do not cite it as Journal of Applied Psychology or as 2020 peer-reviewed (that 2020 item is a different typology review and the preprint). Do not present rho = .16 as causal or as large. Do not say Development-purpose monitoring raises stress (no data). Do not say it is about software engineers.
